title: X Feed Digest
summary: Voice AI was the clearest product theme: OpenAI shipped GPT-Realtime-2 and related speech models, and multiple posts treated voice as a serious agent interface instead of a novelty.
Anthropic had a big distribution-and-capacity day, pushing Claude deeper into Microsoft 365 while also easing Claude Code limits now that more compute is online.
Coding-agent practice is getting sharper: the feed was full of better permission models, model-handoff workflows, and open recipes that make frontier-style agent systems easier to reproduce.

The biggest market-moving headline in the batch was the US trade court ruling against Trump's 10% global tariffs, while Cloudflare layoffs and Google's new wearables push showed AI's pricing and labor effects spreading outward.

items.title: @sama: GPT-Realtime-2 lands in the API
items.body: OpenAI pushed GPT-Realtime-2 into the API and framed voice as becoming the preferred interface when users need to dump lots of context quickly. The bigger takeaway is that realtime voice is moving from gimmick to serious agent surface.

items.title: @claudeai: Claude moves into Microsoft 365
items.body: Anthropic made Claude available directly inside Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, with Outlook in public beta. Carrying context across apps makes the suite feel more like a workflow layer than a standalone chatbot.

items.title: @trq212: Claude Code gets more headroom
items.body: Anthropic says it is rolling back peak-hour limit reductions and doubling Claude Code's 5-hour limits after adding SpaceX compute. That matters because capacity, not raw model quality, has been one of the main bottlenecks for serious coding-agent usage.

items.title: @rwayne: OpenSearch-VL narrows the deep-search moat
items.body: A new OpenSearch-VL release appears to open-source much of the training recipe and data behind frontier multimodal search agents. If the results hold up, closed deep-search systems just lost some defensibility.

items.title: @jun_song: A cleaner Codex handoff loop
items.body: One practical workflow tip stood out: use a stronger planning model to turn project context into a precise Codex prompt, then feed the resulting GitHub output back into the planner for critique and iteration. It is a neat way to spend premium tokens on architecture while keeping execution cheaper.

items.title: @derrickcchoi: Auto-review beats constant approvals
items.body: A useful agent-design point: let coding agents move quickly inside predefined rules, then require review only when they cross risk boundaries. That reduces approval fatigue without giving up the guardrails that keep autonomy safe.

items.title: @WatcherGuru: Trade court blocks Trump's 10% global tariffs
items.body: The most market-relevant headline in the batch was a federal trade court ruling Trump's 10% global tariffs unlawful. If it survives appeal, that removes a meaningful policy overhang for trade-sensitive sectors and global supply chains.

items.title: @Polymarket: Cloudflare cuts 1,100+ jobs
items.body: Reports say Cloudflare is cutting roughly 20% of staff while explicitly framing the move around the "agentic AI era." Even if the messaging is partly narrative management, it is another real example of AI being used to justify cost resets in software.

items.title: @immasiddx: Google takes aim at Whoop
items.body: Google's new Fitbit Air and Google Health stack look like a direct pricing attack on Whoop's subscription-heavy model. The more interesting angle is strategic: Google appears to be making health AI an open, cross-device platform instead of a closed hardware moat.

items.title: @kasong2048: Agents as negotiation labor
items.body: One of the more concrete real-world agent examples: a multi-agent setup ran parallel conversations with more than 10 insurance brokers and reportedly negotiated a better price with almost no human intervention. Agents still struggle with judgment, but they are already very good at tireless coordination in messy, repetitive markets.

items.title: @cholf5: Not every workflow should be a "skill"
items.body: A sharp organizational warning from the batch: if a process is really a fixed SOP, packaging it as a deterministic tool can be cheaper, faster, and more reliable than wrapping it in an LLM. A lot of teams are still overfitting everything into agent-shaped abstractions.

items.title: @GitHub_Daily: Apple Silicon local inference gets a boost
items.body: An open-source framework called Cider is claiming meaningful speed and memory gains for local inference on Apple Silicon, plus an OpenAI-compatible local VLM service. If you run models on a Mac, this was one of the more immediately practical links in the batch.
